items.topic: Refactoring strategy for orchestrator.go DeployDesktop (515-line function)
items.context: The DeployDesktop handler in orchestrator.go is the single worst offender — a 515-line monolith that handles validation, signing, manifest assembly, building, installation, and publishing. This function alone likely accounts for multiple complex_functions violations.

options.label: Extract into sequential phase functions within the same file
options.rationale: Keeps orchestration visible in one file, reduces function complexity. Each phase (validate, sign, assemble, build, publish) becomes a method on the handler struct. Simplest approach, lowest risk.

options.label: Extract phases into separate files with a thin orchestrator
options.rationale: Also reduces file length (1,364 lines). orchestrator.go becomes a ~100-line coordinator calling into deploy_validate.go, deploy_sign.go, etc. Addresses both complex_functions AND long_files violations simultaneously.

items.topic: Platform-specific code splitting for prerequisites.go (1,003 lines)
items.context: prerequisites.go contains platform-specific validation for Windows, macOS, and Linux certificates/prerequisites. Go has native support for build-tag-based file splitting (e.g., prerequisites_windows.go with //go:build windows). However, this code may run cross-platform (validating remote targets), so build tags may not be appropriate.

options.label: Split by platform using Go build tags
options.rationale: Idiomatic Go, cleanest separation. Each platform file only compiles on its target OS. But if the code validates remote targets (not just the local OS), build tags would break cross-compilation.

options.label: Split by platform into separate files without build tags
options.rationale: Reduces file length without build-tag constraints. Files like prerequisites_windows.go, prerequisites_macos.go, prerequisites_linux.go all compile everywhere but organize code by platform. Safe for cross-platform validation scenarios.

options.label: Split by concern (discovery vs. checking vs. remediation)
options.rationale: Groups by function type rather than platform. May produce better abstractions but less intuitive file boundaries.

items.context: The current score is 0 with 151 violations. The plan targets score >= 70 and zero violations across all three categories. Fixing all 151 violations is thorough but may require significant effort. An alternative is to fix the highest-impact violations first to reach a passing score, then address the rest incrementally.

options.label: Fix all 151 violations (target score 100)
options.rationale: Complete cleanup in one pass. No residual tech debt. Most effort upfront but nothing left to revisit.

options.label: Fix top violations to reach score >= 70, then stop
options.rationale: Pragmatic — focuses on the biggest offenders (long files, most complex functions). Remaining minor violations can be addressed in future iterations.

items.topic: UI component extraction approach for GuidedFlow.tsx (513 lines)
items.context: GuidedFlow.tsx is a multi-step wizard with 8 useState hooks, 5 useQuery hooks, and 4 steps rendered inline. It's the longest UI file and likely triggers both complex_functions and long_files violations.

options.label: Extract each step into a sub-component in the same file
options.rationale: Reduces the main component's complexity while keeping related code co-located. Good if steps share significant state.

options.label: Extract each step into its own file in a GuidedFlow/ directory
options.rationale: Maximum file-length reduction. Each step file is ~100-130 lines. Parent component becomes a thin state coordinator. Addresses both complexity and length.

items.text: The deployment-manager has no .golangci.yml configuration. Adding one with funlen, cyclop, and gocognit linters will enforce complexity/length limits going forward and prevent regressions. The refactor skill recommends using tidiness-manager for systematic file tracking during execution.
